## Project Overview

This project demonstrates the application of marketing research and data visualization to understand credit union member perceptions, financial product awareness, and service performance.

The analysis uses Case 31 survey data as an academic alternative to confidential MSDM Culminating Experience Project data.

## Business Objective

Identify opportunities to improve member satisfaction, strengthen competitive positioning, and increase financial product engagement through data-driven decision-making.

## Dataset Overview

| Characteristic | Description |
|---|---|
| Survey respondents | 128 |
| Original variables | 34 |
| Financial products | 14 |
| Interactive visualizations | 3 |
| Dashboard sections | 4 |

## Analytical Methodology

- Descriptive statistical analysis
- Survey data preparation
- Reverse coding
- Composite measurement
- Reliability analysis using Cronbach's alpha
- Financial product awareness analysis
- Geographic segmentation
- Interactive data visualization

## Key Findings

- Overall employee performance averaged **4.21 out of 5**.
- Courtesy received an average rating of **4.35 out of 5**.
- Helpfulness received an average rating of **4.31 out of 5**.
- **59.4%** of respondents provided favorable member-needs ratings.
- Employee performance demonstrated good internal consistency, with a Cronbach's alpha of **0.866**.
- Master credit card had the highest reported product usage at **43.8%**.

## Managerial Recommendations

### Improve Service Performance

Investigate opportunities to improve employee availability and professionalism while maintaining strong courtesy and helpfulness ratings.

### Strengthen Product Engagement

Identify barriers preventing members who are aware of financial products from using them.

### Evaluate Competitive Positioning

Investigate member perceptions of savings rates and compare these perceptions with relevant competitive offerings.

## Limitations

The findings represent descriptive results from an academic survey dataset. Geographic differences should not be interpreted as statistically significant without additional testing.

Only aggregate results are presented. Public distribution remains subject to permission to share the academic case results.
